title: Fourth and fifth declensions

objectives.can: Parse nouns of the fourth and fifth declensions.

explanation.summary: The last two declensions are small. The fourth has a stem in -u and is mostly masculine, with a genitive in -us. The fifth has a stem in -e, is almost all feminine, and has a genitive in -ei. A few of their nouns, among them *spiritus*, *manus*, *dies* and *res*, are among the commonest words of the Bible.

sections.heading: The fourth declension
body: The fourth declension has a stem in -u. Its masculine nouns end in -us in the nominative singular: *spiritus* (spirit), *fructus* (fruit), *exercitus* (army), *vultus* (face), *sensus* (sense), *usus* (use). Two common nouns, *manus* (hand) and *domus* (house), are feminine. There are a few neuters, ending in -u: *cornu* (horn) and *genu* (knee).

The genitive singular ends in -us, and that is the sign: *spiritus, spiritus*. Compare the second declension, where *filius* has the genitive *filii*. A noun in -us whose genitive is -i is second declension; one whose genitive is -us is fourth.

sections.heading: Four forms in -us
body: In the fourth declension the ending -us stands for four different forms: nominative, genitive and vocative singular, and nominative, accusative and vocative plural. It is the least informative ending in Latin. The same is true of -u, which is ablative singular, and in neuters nominative, accusative and vocative.

The library's analysis therefore leaves many of these forms undecided, and the questions below draw only on forms where it was sure. The accusative singular *spiritum*, the dative *spiritui*, the genitive plural *spirituum* and the ablative plural *spiritibus* are clear. The ending -us you must read from the sentence. In *Spiritus Sanctus* the adjective's own ending shows the case: Sanctus is nominative singular, so *spiritus* is too.

sections.heading: The fifth declension
body: The fifth declension has a stem in -e. Its nominative singular ends in -es, and its genitive in -ei. It has few nouns, but they are very common: *dies* (day), *res* (thing, matter), *fides* (faith), *spes* (hope), *facies* (face), *species* (appearance). All are feminine except *dies*, which is masculine or feminine in the singular (feminine especially when it means a fixed day) and masculine in the plural.

Because the nominative singular, nominative plural and accusative plural all end in -es, *dies* and *res* are the same in all three. The singular -em (accusative) and -e (ablative) look like third-declension endings; it is the genitive and dative in -ei that mark the fifth declension. The tables of this lesson show a dash where the analysis is undecided: the genitive singular of *spiritus* is spiritus, that of *dies* is di-ei and that of *res* is r-ei, and the plural nominative and accusative of *dies* and *res* are di-es and r-es.

sections.heading: Nouns that have no plural, or mix declensions
body: Several fifth-declension nouns are rare or absent in the plural: *fides* and *spes* are normally singular, as the forms in the texts show (*fidei*, *spem*). *Dies* and *res* have a full plural: *dierum*, *diebus*, *rerum*, *rebus*.

*Domus* (house) mixes two declensions. Some forms follow the fourth (*domum*, *domibus*), and some follow the second (*domos*, *domorum*, and the form *domi* meaning 'at home'). This is not an error; it is how the word was used. When you read *domum* or *domos*, ask only for the case and number.

misunderstandings: -us does not always mean masculine nominative singular. In the fourth declension it is also the genitive singular and the nominative and accusative plural, and a feminine like *manus* ends in it as well.
A noun in -es is not always third declension. *dies* and *res* are fifth declension, with a genitive in -ei. Check the genitive: -is points to the third declension, -ei to the fifth.
A noun in -u is not necessarily a fourth-declension neuter. The ending -u is also the ablative singular of the masculine *spiritu* and the feminine *manu*.
*dies* is not neuter. It is masculine or feminine, and the adjective beside it shows which.

deeper.heading: How Latin kept these small families
body: In the later language the fourth and fifth declensions shrank. Many fourth-declension nouns went over to the second declension (which is why *domus* has both kinds of form), and most fifth-declension nouns went over to the first. The way *domus* mixes forms is one trace of this. In the texts of this course the standard forms of the common words are by far the most frequent.
